title: The Tech Truce Starts To Fray
gist: A May 2026 Trump-Xi pledge of “constructive strategic stability” has degraded into simmering tension, with the US using the Federal Communications Commission as a new instrument to restrict Chinese tech imports and China answering in early August with deliberately calibrated, non-escalatory counter-restrictions. Gavekal reads this as an uneasy stalemate in which both sides keep unwinding tech dependencies, yet the September Xi-Trump summit still likely proceeds and actual decoupling stays very hard to execute.

themes.theme: FCC as new US tech-restriction tool

insights.claim: The US has begun restricting Chinese technology imports through the Federal Communications Commission, an agency that had not previously been a front-line actor in US-China tech restrictions.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Watch FCC equipment-authorization and covered-list actions, not just Commerce/BIS export controls, as the live channel for new China tech restrictions and the source of headline risk for hardware importers.
insights.quote: the US has tried to restrict Chinese tech imports through a series of measures by a new actor, the Federal Communications Commission
insights.locator: In May, presidents Donald Trump and Xi

insights.claim: A leaders-level pledge of “constructive strategic stability” made in May 2026 did not stop either government from taking new restrictive measures within three months, showing that summit-level detente does not bind the agencies below it.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Treat US-China summit language as a poor predictor of regulatory action; price truce headlines as tactical, and keep hedges on China-exposed tech supply chains through announced detentes.
insights.quote: presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping promised a new era of “constructive strategic stability.” What we have seen since then is a simmering tension
insights.locator: In May, presidents Donald Trump and Xi

insights.claim: China waited until early August 2026 to respond to US technology restrictions, and its counter-measures were deliberately designed to answer the US without escalating.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Beijing's restraint caps near-term tail risk of a full tit-for-tat spiral, arguing against paying up for crash protection on China-linked tech until the calibration pattern breaks.
insights.quote: China finally responded in early August with a calibrated set of its own restrictions, designed to respond to the US but not to escalate.
insights.locator: China finally responded in early August

insights.claim: The underlying US-China relationship is best described as an uneasy stalemate in which both governments continue to look for ways to unwind their mutual technology dependencies, rather than as either a genuine truce or an open conflict.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Structural de-risking spending on both sides is a persistent multi-year bid for domestic-substitute semiconductor, telecom and hardware suppliers regardless of the diplomatic cycle.
insights.quote: the US-China relationship is actually an uneasy stalemate, in which both sides continue to seek ways to unwind their tech dependencies

insights.claim: A Xi-Trump summit scheduled for September 2026 will probably still go ahead because political calculations on both sides favor holding it, despite the recent exchange of technology restrictions.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Fade headlines predicting summit cancellation; a held meeting is the base case and a positioning catalyst for China-exposed risk assets into September.

insights.claim: Practical realities of existing supply chains mean technology decoupling between the US and China will prove very hard to execute, so restriction announcements should not be read as achieved separation.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Expect implementation slippage and carve-outs on decoupling measures; revenue hits to cross-border tech suppliers are likely smaller and slower than policy headlines imply.
